newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain unions, employers present labour reform plans.
newsitem.headline: Spain unions, employers present labour reform plans.

text.p: Spanish unions and employers presented their long-awaited proposals for labour reforms on Wednesday, designed to liberalise one of Europe's most rigid labour markets.
After months of intense talks, which at times verged on collapse, the year-old conservative government breathed a sigh of relief and said it would put the reforms into action as swiftly as possible.
"I am sure these reforms will end the abuse of temporary contracts and provide more stable jobs," Labour Minister Javier Arenas said.

The government hopes the reforms will go part of the way toward cutting its towering unemployment -- the highest in Europe at just under 22 percent -- and preparing the economy for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Leading unions said they were confident their agreed reforms would go a long way toward achieving just that.
"(The deal) is a serious contribution to the improvement of jobs, as well as to the quantity and quality of jobs," Antonio Gutierrez, secretary general of the Workers' Commissions union (CCOO) said.
Employers were also happy with the agreed reforms.

"The union and employer organisations did everything possible...to modernise our economic situation and to ensure a high degree of social stability," Jose Maria Cuevas, president of the employer group CEOE said.
Unions and employers reached a preliminary agreement in March that provided the foundations for a final accord, and have been putting the agreement down on paper since then.
The key feature is a new package of contracts aimed at providing more stability in the labour market and encouraging employers to take on staff.
The centrepiece is a permanent contract which allows for cheaper severance pay -- a key demand of employers.
Employers had complained that Spain's high dismissal costs, among the highest in Europe, dissuaded them from taking on staff under permanent contracts.
As a result the use of temporary contracts exploded and in 1996, 96 percent of new jobs were on temporary contracts, according to the Labour Ministry.
Employers, rather than using the rigid permanent contract, would repeatedly renew temporary contracts.
But this option may no longer be available to employers. The number of contracts that can be used has been reduced to nine from 18.

The new proposed permanent contract is directed toward those areas were unemployment is worst -- among youths, older workers, long-term unemployed and the handicapped -- and those stuck on temporary contracts.
Unions and employers also clarified the reasons that an employer can give for making redundancies. These include economic, technical, productive or organisational reasons.

Employers had previously protested that the reasons were obscure and dismissal cases often ended up in court. In the majority of cases the judge ruled in favour of the employee, forcing employers to pay unfair dismissal costs of 45 days' pay per year worked with a 42-month maximum.

With the polished-up reasons to make redundancies and lower costs for unfair dismissals -- at 33 days' pay per year worked with a maximum of 24 months -- unions are confident temporary contracts will no longer be abused.
The proposals will be a relief to the government which, frustrated by the slow pace of talks, had threatened to step in and impose its own reforms, analysts said.
But the government knew that an accord needed to be voluntary to head off the threat of damaging labour clashes and to be truly effective.
Unions and employers will present the deal for approval by their executive bodies later in April. The deal is expected to be signed at the end of the month.
